Front Office Leaderboard · Active MLB Regimes

How to read a row. Click any regime for its full report card.
  • Channel grades (Draft through Ret): wins above (+) or below (−) what a typical front office got from the same kind of move, per season in the chair. 50 is average on the 20-80 scale; A is about 70+, F under 35. Hover a grade for its number.
  • Overall is the ranking: every channel rolled into one grade of decision quality, leaning on the channels where results repeat (free agency most, trades least). Net wins is the same thing in wins. Success grades results on the field; the gap between Overall and Success is a story in itself.
  • Dev is prospect value created in the org; Ret is whether the players a club let walk did more or less than departures of that caliber usually do.
  • SS small sample (under 3 seasons) · · too few moves to grade (counts as average) · new too new to grade.
Where the numbers come from
  • Every value is Ledger WAR, built here from public data (park factors, defense, framing, baserunning), and only what has already happened on the field counts.
  • Free agency is graded against 2,766 guaranteed contracts; extensions against the league's extensions of the same service class; qualifying-offer signings carry the lost draft pick.
  • The Era filter adds 113 archive regimes (1998-2026), scored by the same engine over their actual windows. The full math and how well it holds up are on the Methodology page.

The Offseason Simulator · Run Your Club's Winter

  • Numbers are wins: the 24-26 slashes are a player's last three seasons, "projects +N" is his 2027, surplus is projected wins net of salary. Dollars are guarantees in $M.

    Methodology

    Reading the numbers, in one minute.
    • Everything is counted in wins, using Ledger WAR, this project's own wins-above-replacement measure built from the public MLB feed. +2.0 WAR means two more team wins than a freely available player.
    • A decision's +/- is what the club got against what a typical front office gets from the same move: a trade at +3.0 brought back three more wins than it gave up; a signing at −2.0 delivered two fewer wins than its price usually buys.
    • Money becomes wins at that year's market price per win. Future wins in a trade are discounted 10% a year.
    • OPEN means players from the decision are still under club control, so the number can still move. Projections are shown beside open deals and never enter a grade.
    • Grades sit on the 20-80 scouting scale: 50 is average, 60 above average, 70 plus, 80 the very top.

    What gets graded, and against what

    The unit is the decision: a dated transaction, credited to the executive regime in office when it was made. Inherited players are not the new regime's; extensions, non-tenders and letting a free agent walk are decisions too. Each channel has its own bar, and a decision is graded only on the gap between what it returned and that bar.

    ChannelWhat the decision earnsThe bar it is measured against
    DraftWins in each pick's club-control seasons (rounds 1-5), wherever he played themThe expected wins for that slot, centered by draft class
    TradesWins received minus wins sent, over each player's window, net of salaryThe other side of the same deal (zero sum)
    Free agencyWins produced for the club in the seasons it held the contractThe cost in wins x what a typical club gets in that contract year, on a deal that size
    ExtensionsArbitration savings in controlled seasons, plus production in the free-agent seasons boughtThe league's average extension of the same service class, per win of cost
    InternationalWins in each signing's control seasonsThe league's realized value per signing in that class
    Waivers / Rule 5Production for the club over the next three seasons (losses charged the same)Zero: pure found money
    RetentionWhat departed free agents did in their next three seasons elsewhereWhat departures of that caliber and age usually do
    DevProspect value created while in the org (top-100 rankings, 2011-26)League average, since development is positive-sum

    Net of cost, always. Free-agent signings and extensions never show raw WAR: signing a star who then plays like a star is a pass, not a triumph. Every graded trade, signing, extension and draft pick also shows its market comps: the three most similar moves league-wide and how they turned out. A trade is graded both as it looked at the time (prospects not yet in the majors carry their rank-curve value from the day of the deal, fading as real seasons replace it) and as it turned out.

    What a free-agent dollar buys, by contract year · wins returned per win of cost at market $/win, every priced free-agent season since 2006. Year one is roughly fair; by year five a club gets half. A deal is graded against these years, not against 1.0.
    The draft bar, by slot · expected wins in club control by overall pick (log scale). The first pick carries a bar of about ten wins; pick 38 about two. A pick is graded against its own slot.

    From net wins to a letter

    Each channel's net is turned into a rate per season in the chair, shrunk toward average for short tenures: rate = net / (seasons + 2). The rate is read in units of that channel's own spread across every graded regime, then placed on the 20-80 scale, so A+ is about the top 5% of a channel and F about the bottom 5%, and a channel too thin to grade counts as average. Overall, the composite, combines the channels into one grade of decision quality and is the leaderboard's ranking. Each channel's net wins count in proportion to how much that channel's results repeat (the second validation check below): weight = 0.5 + 0.5 x the reliability of the full record (Spearman-Brown on the split-half correlation), so free agency counts about 0.73, extensions 0.65, the draft 0.58, waivers 0.52, and trades, international signings and retention 0.5. A channel that is mostly luck still counts, just less. The Net wins column stays the plain, unweighted total. Success grades results on the field (win%, division titles, playoff rounds, pennants, titles) and is kept separate on purpose: a front office can out-decide the league and still miss October, or ride inherited stars to banners. Each single move also carries a letter that ranks it among real moves of the same kind and size, so a $1M signing is judged against $1M signings.

    The value engine (Ledger WAR)

    Every grade is denominated in a wins-above-replacement measure built for this project from the live feed, so no number depends on a licensed source. Offense is linear-weights run value with park factors from each park's home/away run environments (three-year rolling, halved for the road split). Defense, catcher framing and baserunning come from public tracking data; positional credit follows the games actually played at each position. Seasons before 2014 are bat and position only, disclosed wherever they appear. The cache covers 28,460 players, 1998-2026, and is audited for completeness after every refresh. Whether it adds up is tested below.

    Who owns a season: control, contracts and money

    • Club control runs six seasons from the MLB debut (a debut after mid-April runs it one season longer). The decision that acquired a player (the pick, the signing, the trade) owns those seasons wherever he plays them, until a release or a free-agent filing.
    • One contract book holds every guaranteed deal the ledger knows: 2,779 free-agent contracts from the 1997-98 winter on and 826 extensions. A free-agent deal owns its seasons; an extension owns only the seasons beyond the player's original control.
    • Salary is charged at what that money typically buys: a free-agent season at the typical return for its contract year and size (so taking on or shedding a typical contract is neutral, and dumping the last years of a deal is not a windfall). An arbitration season with no contract costs the estimated award: (0.6 + platform WAR) x a class step of 1.0, 1.5 and 3.1 x the $/win drift, calibrated on 48 real 2026 awards (leave-one-out miss about $1.6M). A season lost to injury still charges the salary; cash sent in a trade is charged to the club that paid it.

    Trades: windows, discounting, and no leverage weight

    A traded player is an asset: the acquiring club is credited with his window (six seasons, or to the end of his club control if later) wherever he plays it, so a quick flip is graded in the flip. Future seasons discount 10% a year from the first season of the window, the same for both sides; an October-December deal starts with the next season. Trades are not weighted by playoff leverage: a leverage weight would bill the selling club at the buyer's leverage and move value from bad clubs to good ones by construction (seats on clubs under 72 wins would net −375 wins with such a weight, +33 without). The exclusive right to extend an acquired player is a real asset too: once exercised, the extension's realized surplus is shown beside the trade, and a club that let a star walk is charged the surplus it forfeited, net of the compensation pick.

    Extensions

    An extension is graded against the path it replaced. In seasons the club already controlled, the production belongs to whoever acquired the player; the extension only changes the bill, so it is credited the arbitration salary it replaced (the minimum in pre-arbitration years) and charged its own. In the free-agent seasons it buys, it is a free-agent deal, graded like one. Each service class (pre-debut, early career, arbitration, veteran) is then centered on the league's average result per win of cost for that class, so a club is graded on whom it locked up and at what price, not on which kind of extension it prefers.

    The salary follows the schedule these deals are paid on. Extensions are back-loaded: a few million a year before arbitration, more in arbitration, the bulk in the free-agent years. Charging the average salary every season would make every young player's extension read as a loss in its early years, so the guaranteed total is spread over the seasons in proportion to what each would have cost on the path it replaced (twice the minimum before arbitration, the award model for a 3-win regular or better in arbitration, the average salary in free agency), fixed at signing. Deals still running show a projected finish beside the grade, never in it.

    How an extension is charged, season by season · the same guaranteed total, spread on the schedule these deals are paid on instead of a flat average.

    Retention, conditioned on who left

    Raw leakage (wins departed free agents produce elsewhere) scales with how many stars a club employs, so it would grade payroll, not decisions. The channel conditions on who left: from every free-agent departure 1998-2023 (2,827 with real value behind them), an empirical curve says what departures of each caliber go on to do over their next three seasons (a 2-win departure about 1.5, a 10-win departure about 5.8), adjusted for age (36 and older about half the curve; 29 and under about 1.27x). A regime is graded on the gap between its departures' actual next three seasons and that expectation, plus +1.0 win for each player who declined its qualifying offer and signed elsewhere (the signing club carries the matching charge; the QO table covers 2012-13 through 2025-26). Re-signings and deadline rentals are not departures. Departures after 2023 are excluded until their next three seasons are observable.

    Player development (DEV)

    Prospects are marked to market on a rank-to-surplus-wins curve from the top-100 rankings archive (2011-2026, 1,548 rank-rows), with the holding org taken from minor-league rosters. Entry credit is net of acquisition cost; a prospect developed to the list under a predecessor earns the new regime nothing at entry. Rank moves accrue to the org holding the player, graduation is a neutral exit, falling off without debuting is charged, and credit stays home when the prospect is later traded. Grades are league-relative (about +2.5 wins of prospect value per club-season league-wide).

    Projections (shown, never graded)

    Open deals show a projected finish beside the realized grade. The projection is self-built: a player's WAR rate over the last three seasons weighted 5/4/3, regressed toward his role's league rate by sample size, times expected playing time, then walked forward on aging curves computed from the project's own 28,000-player cache, with attrition. Backtested by projecting each season from only prior data: r = 0.62 (2023) and 0.67 (2025) against actual next-season WAR, mean miss about 0.8 wins. The same projections price contracts: for all 1,607 contracts signed 2010-2025, the suggested terms were rebuilt using only what was known that winter, and set against what each player actually signed for.

    The whole backtest, one dot per signing · Ledger offer vs what the player actually signed for, all 1,607 contracts 2010-2025, both axes log. Dots on the diagonal are priced exactly; hover any dot.

    Validation: does the metric hold up?

    Who watches the Watchmen? A site that grades front offices owes the same scrutiny to its own grades. Three checks, all reproducible from the public feed.

    1. Does it add up? A WAR-class metric must sum to team record. Across all 330 team-seasons 2015-2025, roster-summed Ledger WAR against actual wins above a 48-win replacement baseline: correlation 0.926, R² 0.858, slope 0.915, mean miss 4.8 wins. The slope below 1 reflects known gaps (defense coverage thins before 2016), disclosed rather than patched.

    Roster Ledger WAR vs actual team wins · one dot per team-season, 2015-2025; the dashed line is a perfect match. Hover any dot.

    2. Is a grade skill or luck? Split each regime's decisions (regimes with at least six in a channel) into alternating halves by date and correlate the halves' average result across regimes. If a channel's grade reflects a repeatable skill, a regime's odd-numbered moves should predict its even-numbered ones. Only free agency clears the noise (about ±0.2 at these sample sizes); extensions lean positive; trades, the draft and waivers show no measurable persistence. These numbers set each channel's weight in the Overall grade.

    How much each channel repeats · split-half correlation across regimes (number of regimes in parentheses). Above zero means a club's good moves in that channel tend to come with more good moves.

    3. Does it predict? Pooled across 576 regime-years from 112 regimes (1998-2024), with decision value counted only as it had been realized by each season (no look-ahead), net decision value per season has a partial correlation of 0.11 with the next two seasons' W% after controlling for the record to date; the cluster-bootstrap 95% interval is [-0.01, 0.28], and under grouped 5-fold cross-validation it adds nothing out of sample (R² 0.186 without it, 0.155 with it).

    An honest reading. The letters are an accounting of results: what the decisions returned against what a typical club gets from the same move. They add up, and in free agency they repeat. In trades, the draft and waivers the results are dominated by outcomes no front office controls, so a great trade letter says the trades worked, not that the next one will, and the grades on their own are not a forecast of next year's standings. That is also why short tenures are shrunk toward average.

    Championship provenance

    Every World Series winner 1998-2026 carries a computed roster ledger: core contributors (≥ 1.0 Ledger WAR in the title season) traced to how the club acquired them, split into the sitting regime's moves and what it inherited. Across all 29 titles the median champion was 56% built by its sitting regime, in year 5 of the tenure. Free agency has been the majority channel exactly once (the 2009 Yankees). The median title core was 46% self-built in 1998-2009 and 72% in 2010-2026, yet seven of the seventeen titles since 2010 were won on majority-inherited cores.
